items.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995
items.q: Like downstairs they have those collections — Ethel Waters, Bob Howard, Teddy Wilson

ctx.x: That’s a pretty good analogy. Let me just, before we wrap up, ask, where do you find these tunes?

I get guys to send me tapes. And I buy those things downstairs. Like downstairs they have those collections — Ethel Waters, Bob Howard, Teddy Wilson—I’m just trying to think. You know those, I’ve heard all, not all, but a lot of the greats, the things you hear over and over again. You know the great ones. And then you go looking for oddball stuff to play. And guys make up tapes of oddball things. Cassettes of strange things. I have friends who send me stuff. Wonderful. Tunes I never heard in my life by groups I…

example that Ivy Anderson sang with Ellington and Wingy Manone sang it on records, is “Isn’t Love the Strangest Thing.” You know, pretty melody, everything like that, but I dare say it wouldn’t mean much if you didn’t have a vocal to sing with it. And they say, “Oh gee, what a nice thought,” you know, “how romantic.”
